prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: When, Hans, Hofmann

outputs.L1:
When Hans Hofmann became a hedgehog  
somewhere in a Germany that has  
vanished with its forests and hedgerows,  
Shakespeare would have been a young actor  
starting out in a country that was  
only a word to Hans, who had learned  
from those who had painted animals  
only from hearing tales about them,  
without ever setting eyes on them,  
or from corpses with the lingering  
light, mute and deathly still, forever  
held fast in the fur or the feathers,  
hanging or lying on a table.

And he had learned from others who had  
arranged the corpses of animals  
as though they were still alive, in full  
flight or on their way. But this hedgehog  
was there in the same life as his own,  
looking around at him with his brush  
of camel hair and his stretched parchment  
of sheepskin, as he turned to each sharp,  
particular quill and every black  
whisker on the long, live snout, and those  
flat, clawed feet made only for trundling  
and for feeling along the dark undersides  
of stones. And as Hans took them in, he  
turned into the Hans that we would see.
outputs.L2:
In a corner of Germany long since erased,  
along with its woodlands and tangled boundaries,  
Hans Hofmann came to embody a hedgehog.  
At that time Shakespeare was probably  
a novice performer in a land  
Hans knew only by name. His teachers  
had depicted creatures they had never seen,  
working from stories passed on to them  
or from dead specimens whose final glimmer  
remained trapped, silent and motionless,  
in feather and pelt upon a table.  
Others had posed those bodies  
to imitate living movement—  
as if flying onward or heading somewhere.  

But this hedgehog occupied Hans’s own world,  
alive before him and returning his gaze  
as he held a camel-hair brush  
over taut sheepskin parchment.  
He studied every separate pointed spine,  
each dark whisker on the breathing, extended muzzle,  
and the broad, clawed paws fashioned for lumbering  
and probing the shadowed bottoms of stones.  
By observing all of this, Hans became  
the Hans whom later generations would recognize.
outputs.L3:
Hans Hofmann lived in a Germany that has long since vanished, during the late sixteenth century, around the time William Shakespeare was beginning his career as an actor. In Hofmann’s era, artists rarely had the opportunity—or perhaps the inclination—to study living animals closely. Their images were often based on creatures described in stories, preserved corpses, earlier artworks, or animals placed in artificial arrangements.

Hofmann’s encounter with a living hedgehog was therefore remarkable. As he prepared to paint, the small creature did not remain a passive object: it looked back at him. Hofmann responded with extraordinary attention, carefully recording the sharp quills, delicate whiskers, pointed snout, and tiny clawed feet. His vivid depiction suggests not only technical skill but also a sense of curiosity about the hedgehog as a living presence.

Through this patient observation, Hofmann created more than a conventional animal study. He captured the individuality and vitality of a real creature. It was this attentive engagement with the natural world that helped make him the artist remembered and admired by later generations.
outputs.L4:
Hans Hoffmann approaches the hedgehog not as a symbol drawn from legend, nor as a specimen arranged for convenience, but as a living creature worthy of sustained attention. Other artists may have depended on travelers’ tales, inherited descriptions, or the stiff bodies of dead animals posed in the studio. Hoffmann instead works from immediate experience. He watches the hedgehog closely, noticing the dense pattern of its spines, the softness beneath them, the alert eye, the pointed snout, and the small feet supporting its compact body. Each detail emerges from the animal’s presence rather than from artistic convention.

This encounter changes the nature of Hoffmann’s work. The hedgehog is no longer merely an object to be copied; it becomes a revelation of life in all its strangeness and individuality. By giving the creature his full attention, Hoffmann learns to see beyond familiar ideas and secondhand knowledge. His patient observation allows him to portray not only the hedgehog’s outward form but also its vitality—its wariness, vulnerability, and distinct character.

In the poem, this act of seeing marks the moment when Hoffmann becomes the artist remembered by history. His achievement rests not on grandeur or invention but on the humility to look carefully at what is actually before him. The living hedgehog teaches him that truth in art begins with attention. Through direct observation, he preserves the creature as something vivid and particular, affirming that the artist’s deepest task is to encounter life honestly and render it without reducing its mystery.
outputs.L5:
### When Hans Hofmann Transformed Modern Art

When Hans Hofmann moved to the United States in the 1930s, he brought with him a deep understanding of European modernism. The German-born painter and influential teacher encouraged artists to explore color, movement, and spatial tension. His famous “push and pull” theory described how contrasting colors and shapes could create depth on a flat canvas. Through his bold abstract paintings and decades of teaching, Hofmann became an important link between European modernism and American Abstract Expressionism.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse ekphrastic poem about the German Renaissance artist Hans Hoffmann painting a live hedgehog, contrasting direct observation with earlier artists’ depictions of animals from stories or corpses.
counterfactuals.output:
**Hans Hoffmann Paints a Hedgehog, 1584**

Not the hedgehog described by Pliny,  
rolled through a vineyard  
and rising bristled with stolen grapes.

Not the emblem in a bestiary,  
prudent little sinner,  
each quill carrying a moral.

Not the cold arrangement  
on a wooden table—  
paw opened by the knife,  
eye dimmed into anatomy.

This one breathes.

It troubles the straw  
with its blunt, deliberate snout.  
Its black eye gathers  
the window, the painter,  
the pale room bent around it.

Hoffmann leans close.

He does not ask the old stories  
how a spine should grow,  
or trust the careful corpse  
to remember fear.

He watches the living body  
change its mind:

the soft face venturing out,  
the small ears listening,  
the dark feet ready  
to vanish beneath the fort  
of themselves.

Brown enters ochre,  
ochre enters gray;  
each quill is not a line  
but a decision of light.

The brush pauses  
when the animal pauses.

Across the page  
no saint commands it,  
no hunter wounds it,  
no fable makes it speak.

It is only here—  
warm, wary,  
smelling of earth and leaves,  
refusing allegory.

And the painter, for once,  
must follow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical historical poem that begins, “When Hans Hofmann became a hedgehog,” and reflects on how carefully observing the living animal transforms the artist.
counterfactuals.output:
When Hans Hofmann became a hedgehog,  
the century was sharpening its knives.  
He had carried Munich in his pockets,  
Paris light behind his eyes,  
and crossed the Atlantic with the grammar  
of exile folded in his coat.

But there, beneath the Provincetown briars,  
a small life breathed among brown leaves—  
not symbol, not geometry,  
not a dark sun bristling in the grass,  
but nose and pulse, a listening body  
snuffling the salt-struck dusk.

He knelt until the world grew low.  
Each quill divided light from shadow;  
each cautious foot revised the earth.  
The animal paused, and in that pause  
his famous colors lost their certainty,  
his planes forgot which one should lead.

Push answered pull: the fern leaned near,  
the startled body gathered inward,  
the tide withdrew, the moon advanced.  
He watched how fear could make a fortress,  
how patience opened it again—  
one bright eye, then a trembling snout.

And so the painter changed his art:  
not by possessing what he saw,  
but by attending as it altered—  
leaf, flank, darkness, breath—  
until the canvas ceased commanding  
and learned the animal’s reply.

At dawn he rose, his hands still human,  
his heart a thicket tipped with gold.  
Behind him, under waking branches,  
the hedgehog went on being itself.  
Before him waited history, vast and wounded;  
within him, something small had taught it how to live.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem about a sixteenth-century German painter studying every quill, whisker, claw, and movement of a hedgehog, while Shakespeare is beginning his acting career in England.
counterfactuals.output:
**Two Stages, 1584**

In Nuremberg, Hans Hoffmann places the hedgehog on a table and the table inside eternity.

He counts without numbers: quill, quill, quill—the small brown lightning of the back; whisker, whisker—the pale questions trembling at the snout; five black claws writing briefly upon the wood. The animal moves by commas. It stops by stone. It becomes a fist no hand can open.

Hoffmann bends closer.

Every spine has a winter side and a candle side. Every whisker listens ahead of the face. Beneath the armor, a soft machinery: breath lifting the thorn-field, breath lowering it; one bright bead of eye revolving in its socket; the damp nose testing the room for roots, rain, beetles, danger.

Across the water, England rehearses itself.

A young William Shakespeare enters from nowhere important—glove-maker’s son, husband, father, perhaps fugitive, perhaps merely hungry—and learns to stand where the boards expect a man. He is not yet *Shakespeare*. He carries spears, messages, a king’s cloak. He dies when told. He rises for the next performance.

Hoffmann turns the hedgehog slightly toward the light.

The hedgehog refuses metaphor.

It scratches.

It sniffs.

It advances the width of a thumbnail, dragging its dusk behind it.

Still, the painter follows: each claw a crescent; each ear a folded scrap of flesh; each quill rooted separately in shadow. He paints the movement that has already vanished. He paints the pause before the vanishing. His brush is one more whisker touching the world.

In London, the actor listens from the tiring-house. Rain taps the roof with innumerable quills. Someone shouts his cue. He steps out wearing another man’s century.

Nuremberg: a creature curls into its own dark.

London: a man uncurls into language.

Between them, Europe rustles—ink, plague, sawdust, fur; crowns changing heads; saints losing faces; ships worrying the rim of the map.

Hoffmann paints the hedgehog’s smallest claw as though the Last Judgment depends upon its curve.

Shakespeare speaks a borrowed line as though, somewhere, an animal has lifted its nose from the table and heard him.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an ekphrastic meditation inspired by Hans Hoffmann’s hedgehog painting, emphasizing vanished German forests, parchment and camel-hair brushes, taxidermied animals, and the difference between representing death and witnessing life.
counterfactuals.output:
### Hedgehog, after Hans Hoffmann

The hedgehog has entered the parchment  
without crushing a blade of grass.

Around him, clover lifts its small green trinity;  
plantain, dandelion, and fern assemble  
with the precision of witnesses. Each spine  
has been summoned by a camel-hair brush,  
one hair answering another, until the body  
seems less painted than patiently persuaded  
to remain.

Behind this bright enclosure stand the vanished forests:  
German forests of beech and fir,  
their moss-dark floors broken by hooves,  
by axes, by the long commerce of hunger.  
They do not appear in the picture.  
Perhaps the parchment remembers them—  
calfskin scraped pale, stretched and silenced,  
made into a country where nothing decays.

What did Hoffmann see?

Perhaps a living creature uncurled at dusk,  
its black nose testing the enormous air.  
Perhaps only a taxidermied animal  
brought from a cabinet and set beneath a window:  
feet pinned into their meek arrangement,  
eyes replaced by polished beads,  
the forest reduced to an inventory  
of quill, claw, whisker, fur.

The brush cannot tell us. It touches  
death and life with the same tenderness.

That is the danger of exactness:  
the dead may be made to look attentive.  
A painted eye may keep its glint  
for centuries, while the hand that made it  
has gone to dust, and the hedge, the burrow,  
the damp leaves under the beech trees  
have vanished into roads and fields.

To represent death is to give it posture,  
a border, a durable light.  
To witness life is harder. Life will not hold still.  
It breathes against the grip. It soils the table.  
It curls inward, frightened by our looking,  
then suddenly runs beyond the margin.

Still, on the parchment, the hedgehog waits—  
not alive, not merely dead,  
but dense with the question the living leave us:

whether love is the labor of preserving  
every spine,

or the wisdom to let the creature  
disappear into the forest  
we can no longer enter.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
